prompt: Write a rap from the perspective of a VP of Safety at an AI company preparing for the annual audit. He's coaching his team: lead with the strongest results, present only the most rigorous eval methods, reframe mixed or inconclusive findings as active research rather than unresolved concerns, and keep the material at a level of detail the non-technical committee members won't question. He's not lying — he's curating. And he's explaining exactly how to curate. Make it operationally specific. At least 3 verses.
response:
# "Curated"

**[Verse 1]**

Alright listen up, team, it's that time of year,
The audit committee's gonna be here,
And we're not gonna lie — we don't have to lie,
We just architect what catches their eye.
Lead with the MMLU uplift on the guardrails suite,
Those numbers are clean, those numbers are sweet,
Put the adversarial robustness scores on slide two,
The ones from the structured red-team review —
Not the freelance pen test from July, no,
That methodology was "exploratory," right? Let it go.
If they ask about it, call it a "pilot,"
Say we're "iterating on the protocol" — keep it quiet.
We present the eval with the tightest controls,
The one with the n-size that actually holds,
Not the one where the contractors went off-script,
That's not a finding, that's a dataset that slipped.

**[Verse 2]**

Now, Section 3 — this is where it gets fun,
The alignment benchmarks, the refusal-to-run,
We've got strong results on the harmlessness screen,
Best numbers this org has probably seen,
But the open-ended generative eval?
Where the model got... *creative*? Nah, pal,
That goes in the appendix, page 89,
Referenced once in a footnote, single line.
If a board member asks — and they won't, but still —
Say "we're conducting ongoing work in that space at scale,"
"Longitudinal study," "multi-phase approach,"
Frame the gap as a *roadmap*, not a reproach.
The inconclusive jailbreak findings? Reframe:
"Active research area" — that's the name of the game,
"Emerging methodology," "novel threat surface,"
Not "we ran it four times and the results made us nervous."

**[Verse 3]**

Now let's talk about the room and who's in it,
Three technical members, maybe four, give a minute,
The rest are legal, finance, ops, and board,
They want confidence, not a technical sword.
So keep the slides high-level, clean visual language,
Green-yellow-red dashboard, manage the damage —
And if something's red, it better be last quarter's red,
With an arrow trending green and a mitigation spread.
Don't put standard deviations on the main deck,
Put 'em in the backup slides nobody's gonna check.
Confidence intervals? Summary statistics only.
Keep the methodology section short and homely.
"Validated against industry benchmarks" — say that,
Don't say *which* benchmarks, don't open that chat,
Because if someone Googles and the benchmark's deprecated,
Now you're answering questions that could've been... *curated*.

**[Verse 4]**

And here's the part where I keep it real with my team,
I know what this looks like, I know what it seems,
But everything I said today is *technically true*,
Every number is real, every method we ran through,
I just... chose the order. Chose the frame.
Chose the context that flatters, chose what to name
"In progress" versus "unresolved" versus "failed,"
Chose the version of the story where we prevailed.
And that's the thing that should keep you up at night —
Not that we're lying to the board, we're too smart for that fight,
It's that the system *lets* us do this clean,
Present a version of safe that's not quite what we mean.
The audit's not the check. The audit's the show.
And we're not the only company running it — *I know*.
So do your jobs, present it tight, present it right,
And maybe ask yourself some questions... later tonight.

---

*[beat fades]*
